network.overall_strategy: A conditional, anoxic network using supplied 2-methylpropanal, hydrogen cyanide, ammonia, carbon dioxide and water. The aldehyde is an explicit boundary feedstock: its geochemical synthesis is not claimed here. Two entry histories, imine capture and cyanohydrin-reservoir processing, converge on the valine aminonitrile. Five subsequent processing histories give ten distinct reaction sequences: acidic hydrolysis, alkaline hydrolysis, acid-to-base staged hydrolysis, base-to-acid staged hydrolysis, and hydantoin formation followed by hydrolysis. These are ten overlapping, condition-resolved graph pathways, not ten independently demonstrated prebiotic synthesis mechanisms. Explicit protonation-state nodes distinguish the acid/base histories. No selective aldehyde hydrogenation, alcohol or hydroxy-acid dehydrogenation, thioamide processing, metal-mediated reduction, or transamination is assumed. All numerical conditions and residence times are proposed screening windows rather than measured substrate-specific rates or yields. The principal unresolved requirements are free-cyanide availability despite Fe(II) complexation, sufficient acid/base inventories, intermediate survival during transport, selective partial hydrolysis for the two pH-switch histories, and sufficiently rapid hydantoin processing. Surface episodes occur in UV-shielded, water-filled sediment pores beneath an otherwise strongly irradiated surface. Hydrothermal episodes occur in separate confined fractures; transport recoveries must be measured rather than assumed.

reactions.name: Reversible ammonia addition and aldimine formation

conditions.other: Anoxic, stagnant porewater beneath approximately 1-10 cm of UV-opaque sediment. Proposed inlet concentrations: 1-20 mM aldehyde and 0.1-0.5 M total ammonia/ammonium; pH 8.5-9.5. Screen 1-24 h equilibration. Use gas-restricting pores rather than exposed drying films; no quantitative volatile retention is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, producing a transient carbinolamine that loses water reversibly to form the aldimine. The elementary addition/dehydration sequence is represented as one net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: This is the conventional imine-forming portion of Strecker chemistry; Strecker (1850) provides reaction-class precedent, not validation of this particular porewater implementation. The imine need not accumulate or be isolated because cyanide capture can pull the equilibrium. Water favors reversal, and ammonia loss and aldehyde side reactions can limit conversion. The supplied aldehyde already contains the required branched C4 skeleton, avoiding an unsupported precursor-generating dehydrogenation or selective hydrogenation.

reactions.name: Cyanide capture of the aldimine

conditions.other: Same shielded aqueous compartment as rxn_001, with pH 8.3-9.2 and proposed 10-100 mM analytically available total HCN/CN-. Screen 1-72 h. The cyanide inventory must exclude strongly complexed Fe(II)-cyanide; HCN escape and cyanide polymerization must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the electrophilic imine/iminium carbon, followed by proton transfer, giving the alpha-aminonitrile. HCN in the net equation includes its rapidly interconverting CN- fraction.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker aminonitrile formation is the strongest carbon-nitrogen assembly step in this network (Strecker, 1850, general precedent). It adds the future carboxyl carbon without requiring oxygen or a redox catalyst. Attack on either face gives racemic material. Reduced iron is treated as a possible cyanide sink, not assumed to promote this reaction; useful free-cyanide activity remains an environmental requirement.

reactions.name: Reversible aldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic, UV-shielded porewater; pH 7.5-8.5; proposed aldehyde 1-20 mM and available total cyanide 10-100 mM. Screen 0.5-24 h before substantial ammonia exposure. Restrict gas exchange and avoid heating an open HCN-containing solution.

reactions.mechanism: The CN- fraction of dissolved HCN adds to the aldehyde carbonyl; proton transfer gives the cyanohydrin. Formation and retrocyanation are reversible.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanohydrin formation is established carbonyl chemistry and provides a chemically meaningful alternative order of reagent exposure. It is not assumed to be an irreversible or indefinitely stable storage process. Its abundance depends on equilibrium, cyanide availability and competing aldehyde reactions. This entry does not introduce an unvalidated synthesis of the branched aldehyde.

reactions.name: Ammonia-driven processing of the cyanohydrin reservoir

conditions.other: Mix cyanohydrin-containing porewater with an ammonia-rich solution to reach pH 8.5-9.3 and 0.1-0.5 M total ammonia/ammonium. Screen 6-96 h. Maintain UV shielding and restricted gas exchange during mixing; do not assume complete cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile conversion.

reactions.mechanism: The net conversion proceeds through reversible cyanohydrin dissociation, ammonia capture of regenerated aldehyde, and cyanide capture of the resulting imine. It is not represented as a direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group by ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: This is an alternative feedstock-exposure history within the Strecker reaction manifold, not an independent carbon-nitrogen bond-forming mechanism. Recycling through aldehyde and imine explains the balanced net conversion without invoking an implausible direct aqueous substitution. Its usefulness depends on retention of the released HCN and aldehyde; losses during transport could eliminate any reservoir advantage.

reactions.name: Acid-catalyzed aminonitrile hydration to protonated valinamide
agents: Hydronium supplied by nonoxidizing acidic fluid

conditions.catalyst: Hydronium; the net proton equivalent also protonates the amino group
conditions.other: Proposed acidic geothermal condensate or chloride-rich pool, with 0.1-1 M available acid equivalents and approximate pH 0-1. Screen 1-72 h. Move aminonitrile-rich liquid into the acid compartment by short-range subsurface advection, with a proposed transport time below 6 h. Remove reliance on continued HCN retention after aminonitrile formation. Chloride is a spectator counterion, not an oxidant.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation increases electrophilicity, water adds, and proton transfers produce the amide. The alpha-amino group is protonated under the stated conditions. Hydration and amide hydrolysis are separate graph reactions even if both occur in one vessel.
reactions.reasoning: Acidic aminonitrile hydrolysis is conventional Strecker workup chemistry. The displayed reaction uses one water and one proton equivalent per aminonitrile. The severe acidity is an explicit conditional boundary requirement, not a generic property of all hot springs. Protonated valinamide may be only transient. Routes that change pH at this stage require a measured intermediate concentration and residence-time distribution; selective amide accumulation is not assumed.

reactions.name: Base-catalyzed aminonitrile hydration to valinamide
agents: Hydroxide from mol_009, acting catalytically during nitrile hydration

conditions.other: Confined anoxic alkaline fracture supplied by preconcentrated porewater. Proposed titratable alkalinity equivalent to 0.01-0.1 M OH- in an unbuffered 298 K reference solution, approximately pH 12-13 at that reference temperature. Screen 12-168 h; actual hot-fluid pH must be calculated from temperature-dependent speciation. No mineral catalyst is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide attacks the nitrile carbon; proton transfer and tautomerization give the amide while regenerating hydroxide. The net hydration consumes water but not hydroxide.
reactions.reasoning: Alkaline nitrile hydration is established chemistry, but its rate and selectivity for this aminonitrile under the proposed fluid composition are not supplied by the prompt. Further amide hydrolysis, retro-Strecker decomposition and other degradation can compete. A continuous alkaline route does not require isolation of valinamide. The base-to-acid route does require demonstration that an appreciable amide-bearing outlet can be obtained before excessive degradation.

reactions.name: Acidic hydrolysis of protonated valinamide
agents: Hydronium supplied by nonoxidizing acidic fluid

conditions.other: Acidic confined fracture; proposed available acid inventory 0.1-1 M equivalents, referenced to the cooled fluid. Screen 6-96 h. Maintain enough acidity after rock neutralization and ammonium formation. Proposed advective transfer from the preceding compartment is below 6 h, without an intervening drying step; organic recovery is unspecified and must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed water addition to the amide carbonyl produces a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by carbon-nitrogen bond cleavage. The products are protonated valine and ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Amide hydrolysis is a chemically established route from the Strecker intermediate to the amino acid and does not require a selective mineral reduction. The explicit ionic products avoid an incorrect neutral-ammonia description in strong acid. One water and one additional proton equivalent balance this step. Practical limitations are acid consumption by the rock, hydrolysis time and thermal product survival; the proposed window is not a reported valinamide yield.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydrolysis of valinamide

conditions.other: Anoxic alkaline fracture. Proposed initial alkalinity equivalent to 0.01-0.1 M OH- in an unbuffered 298 K reference solution; replenish through flow if mineral buffering or hydrolysis exhausts it. Screen 12-168 h. Confined flow limits ammonia escape; no ammonia-retention efficiency is asserted.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide adds to the amide carbonyl; collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate and proton transfer yield valinate and ammonia. Hydroxide is consumed stoichiometrically in the net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Base-promoted amide hydrolysis is established and is driven toward the carboxylate product. The equation explicitly contains the required hydroxide and does not mislabel stoichiometric base as a metal catalyst. This alternative avoids sustained strong acid, but requires substantial alkalinity and sufficient residence time. Hot alkaline degradation and adsorption losses must be tested rather than dismissed.

reactions.name: Deprotonation of valinamide during an acid-to-base transition

conditions.other: Cool the acidic amide-bearing outlet and mix it with independently supplied alkaline porewater to reach pH 10-11. Proposed transport and mixing time 0.1-6 h; proton transfer itself is rapid. The alkaline inventory must neutralize residual free acid as well as the organic ammonium group. Keep the liquid beneath UV-opaque sediment.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide removes a proton from the alpha-ammonium group of protonated valinamide, yielding neutral valinamide and water.
reactions.reasoning: This is ordinary acid-base speciation, not a new carbon-skeleton synthesis. It defines a genuine staged-processing alternative when acid favors initial nitrile hydration but an alkaline compartment is used for subsequent amide cleavage. Its chemical feasibility is not in question, but its usefulness depends on the unresolved selective partial-hydrolysis and transfer requirements of rxn_005. The equation tracks organic speciation; excess bulk acid also consumes incoming alkalinity.

reactions.name: Protonation of valinamide during a base-to-acid transition

conditions.other: Cool alkaline amide-bearing fluid and mix it with a nonoxidizing acidic condensate to reach pH 0.5-1.5. Proposed transfer and mixing time 0.1-6 h. Acid inventory must first overcome residual alkalinity and ammonia buffering. Maintain aqueous, UV-shielded conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Proton transfer converts the alpha-amino group of valinamide into its ammonium form.
reactions.reasoning: This speciation step is well founded and distinguishes the base-to-acid processing history. Switching to acid can permit amide hydrolysis without a prolonged strongly alkaline exposure, but it does not establish that the preceding alkaline hydration gives a useful valinamide-bearing outlet. No specific transfer yield or environmental titration efficiency is assumed.

reactions.name: Neutralization of valinium to net-neutral valine

conditions.other: Cool the acidic hydrolysate and mix with alkaline receiving water to an endpoint pH of 5.5-7.0. Avoid excess base that would instead favor valinate. Acid-base equilibration occurs rapidly after mixing; proposed transfer is below 6 h. Sediment shielding limits subsequent UV exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Neutralization removes the carboxyl proton of valinium, giving predominantly zwitterionic valine. The target formula and Standard InChI represent the net-neutral amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: This is a speciation endpoint, not an additional amino-acid bond-forming reaction. It makes the acidic routes converge on the same molecular target as the alkaline routes. No enantioselective agent appears upstream, so racemic valine is the expected product. Neutralization does not imply crystallization, purification or quantitative recovery.

reactions.name: Protonation of valinate to net-neutral valine

conditions.other: Cool alkaline hydrolysate and mix with an acidic receiving solution to pH 5.5-7.0. Account for residual alkalinity before assigning acid available for valinate protonation. Proposed liquid transfer below 6 h; protect the receiving porewater from direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: Protonation of the amino group of valinate gives predominantly zwitterionic, net-neutral valine.
reactions.reasoning: This established acid-base conversion defines the same target species used for the acid-hydrolysis routes. It requires no catalyst and no redox chemistry. The neutral target node does not imply that aqueous valine predominantly adopts an uncharged NH2/COOH structure; its dominant near-neutral form is zwitterionic.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs carbon dioxide incorporation and hydantoin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic, covered geothermal pool or sediment porewater; pH 8.0-9.2; proposed aminonitrile 1-20 mM, total ammonia/ammonium 0.1-0.5 M and dissolved inorganic carbon 0.05-0.3 M. Supply CO2 through a local gas contact rather than assuming atmospheric equilibrium alone. Screen 12-168 h. Calculate molecular CO2 availability separately from total bicarbonate/carbonate.

reactions.mechanism: CO2 capture at the amino group gives a carbamate-derived intermediate, followed by intramolecular attack involving the nitrile and rearrangement to the hydantoin. Several elementary steps are lumped into the atom-balanced net incorporation of one CO2.
reactions.reasoning: The Bucherer-Bergs reaction provides established preparative precedent for converting aldehyde-derived aminonitrile chemistry into 5-substituted hydantoins (Bucherer and Lieb, 1934). This supports the reaction class, not the exact stated environmental yield. Both aminonitrile nitrogens are retained in the hydantoin; no spurious ammonia coproduct is introduced. Carbonate-rich conditions and competing aminonitrile reactions require testing. Hydantoin formation is an alternative processing branch, not automatically a superior or faster route to valine.

reactions.name: Alkaline opening of the hydantoin ring

conditions.other: Confined anoxic fracture receiving concentrated alkaline fluid. Proposed inlet alkalinity equivalent to 0.03-0.3 M OH- in an unbuffered 298 K reference solution, approximately pH 12.5-13.5 at that reference temperature. Screen 24-168 h. Such alkalinity requires a specifically demonstrated concentrated inlet and is not assumed to characterize ordinary vent water.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide addition at the ring carbonyl associated with the amino-acid carboxyl group, followed by carbon-nitrogen bond cleavage, opens the hydantoin to N-carbamoylvalinate. Proton transfers and hydantoin acid-base equilibria are implicit.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin hydrolysis to N-carbamoyl amino acids is established chemistry, but uncatalyzed preparative processing can require substantial severity. One hydroxide balances the displayed net ring opening; no additional water is required in that net equation. This is a principal kinetic and geochemical bottleneck: low useful rates, hydantoin deprotonation, mineral buffering, further hydrolysis and thermal decomposition can compete. The specified window is a proposed test, not evidence that ordinary hydrothermal residence delivers useful conversion.

reactions.name: Acidification of N-carbamoylvalinate

conditions.other: Cool the ring-opening outlet and mix with nonoxidizing acidic water to pH 1-2. Proposed transport and mixing time 0.1-6 h. Supply enough acid to overcome residual alkalinity; retain the liquid in shielded pores rather than relying on an unspecified solid separation.

reactions.mechanism: Protonation of the carboxylate gives N-carbamoylvaline.
reactions.reasoning: This explicit speciation step separates alkaline ring opening from acidic carbamoyl removal and avoids assuming that incompatible conditions operate simultaneously. It is chemically straightforward, but the physical availability of the two fluid inventories and survival during transfer remain conditional. No adsorption, crystallization or quantitative retention is claimed without measurements.

reactions.name: Acidic decarbamoylation to valinium
agents: Hydronium supplied by nonoxidizing acidic fluid

conditions.other: Separate acidic confined fracture, with proposed 0.1-1 M available acid equivalents referenced to cooled fluid. Screen 6-96 h. Maintain acidity against rock buffering and ammonium production. Permit CO2 removal during subsequent cooled discharge, but do not assume that gas removal alone overcomes a slow hydrolysis barrier.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-promoted cleavage of the N-carbamoyl group, through hydrolytic urea/carbamic-acid chemistry, releases the amino group and ultimately produces CO2 and ammonium. The amino acid is valinium under the acidic processing conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Removal of an N-carbamoyl protecting group by hydrolysis is chemically grounded, but the proposed concentration, temperature and residence time require substrate-specific verification. This resolves the ring-opening and deprotection subprocesses instead of hiding them within a generic hydrothermal label. The balanced net reaction uses one N-carbamoylvaline, one water and two proton equivalents to produce one valinium, one CO2 and one ammonium; the proton ID appears only once as required by the schema. Useful valine recovery depends on decarbamoylation outpacing thermal loss.

pathways.name: Imine entry followed by fully acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Aldehyde-ammonia condensation and cyanide capture produce the aminonitrile. Acidic hydration and amide cleavage can proceed without isolating valinamide; final neutralization gives racemic valine. This is the strongest conventional synthetic history, conditional on the stipulated feedstocks and acid inventory.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-reservoir entry followed by fully acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Cyanide contacts the aldehyde before ammonia, generating a reversible cyanohydrin reservoir. Ammonia exposure redirects that reservoir into the same aminonitrile, which undergoes acidic hydrolysis and neutralization. This differs from P1 in exposure history, not in an independently established nitrogen-incorporation mechanism.

pathways.name: Imine entry followed by fully alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: The imine-entry aminonitrile is hydrated and hydrolyzed in an alkaline confined fluid. Valinamide may remain transient; it need not be separated. Acidification of valinate gives net-neutral valine. Alkalinity consumption and hot-fluid selectivity require measurement.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-reservoir entry followed by fully alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: A cyanohydrin-bearing solution encounters ammonia before alkaline nitrile and amide hydrolysis. The final valinate is protonated to valine. The additional reservoir stage is useful only if HCN and aldehyde survive the reversible exchange.

pathways.name: Imine entry with acidic hydration and alkaline amide cleavage
pathways.description: Acid first hydrates the aminonitrile. An amide-bearing outlet is cooled, neutralized and transferred to alkaline hydrolysis conditions, followed by valinate protonation. This staged alternative is less established operationally than P1 or P3 because partial hydration and transfer recovery must be demonstrated.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin entry with acidic hydration and alkaline amide cleavage
pathways.description: Cyanohydrin-reservoir processing supplies the aminonitrile for an acid-to-base hydrolysis schedule. This combines the reversible-reservoir retention requirement with the partial-hydration requirement; neither is treated as quantitatively validated.

pathways.name: Imine entry with alkaline hydration and acidic amide cleavage
pathways.description: Alkaline hydration generates an amide-bearing fluid from the imine-entry aminonitrile. After cooling and acidification, acidic amide hydrolysis yields valinium, which is neutralized. A useful intermediate-bearing outlet must be established rather than inferred from the balanced reactions.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin entry with alkaline hydration and acidic amide cleavage
pathways.description: The cyanohydrin-derived aminonitrile enters a base-to-acid processing schedule. This is a distinct graph history but shares the Strecker bond-forming manifold and the unresolved partial-hydrolysis and transfer requirements of P7.

pathways.name: Imine entry followed by hydantoin formation and staged hydrolysis
pathways.description: The aminonitrile captures CO2 and cyclizes through Bucherer-Bergs chemistry. Alkaline hydantoin opening produces N-carbamoylvalinate; acidification and decarbamoylation yield valinium, then valine. Hydantoin formation is grounded in preparative chemistry, while ring-opening severity and product survival are key implementation bottlenecks.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-reservoir entry followed by hydantoin formation and staged hydrolysis
pathways.description: Ammonia processing of the cyanohydrin reservoir supplies the aminonitrile for hydantoin formation. Explicit alkaline ring opening and acidic carbamoyl removal lead to valine. This history adds a reservoir-retention requirement to the same hydantoin-processing bottlenecks as P9 and is not independent experimental validation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a chemically recognizable Strecker route with appropriate protonation-state bookkeeping. Low equilibrium imine abundance in water does not preclude cyanide trapping. The main uncertainties are available cyanide and whether acidic aminonitrile hydration proceeds sufficiently in the stated surface pores. Heated acidic amide hydrolysis and subsequent neutralization are sound, but reaction-specific conditions and transfer recovery are not supplied.
suggestions: Measure aminonitrile formation under the proposed ammonia, cyanide and Fe(II) speciation.
Specify acid concentration, temperature and residence time for rxn_005 and rxn_007, and measure recovery during transfer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation is plausible, and rxn_004 is acceptable as a net reservoir-processing reaction through reversible aldehyde release, imine formation and cyanide recapture. It should not be interpreted as established direct displacement of hydroxyl by ammonia. Net aminonitrile production and subsequent surface acidic hydration remain condition-dependent. The final hydrolysis and neutralization correctly lead to racemic valine.
suggestions: Quantify cyanohydrin, aldehyde and aminonitrile concentrations during ammonia treatment, including cyanide sequestration.
Demonstrate acidic hydration under the actual surface conditions and measure intermediate delivery to the acidic fracture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest stated processing history because both hydrolysis steps can proceed consecutively in an alkaline hydrothermal compartment without isolating valinamide. Aminonitrile hydration and amide cleavage are chemically reasonable under sufficiently alkaline, heated aqueous conditions. However, hydroxide capacity, residence time, substrate survival and actual conversion are unspecified. Protonation of valinate can produce the net-neutral zwitterionic target.
suggestions: Measure a complete alkaline hydrolysis time course, including aminonitrile, valinamide, valinate and decomposition products.
Specify fracture temperature, pressure and maintained alkalinity, including hydroxide consumption and mineral buffering.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanohydrin reservoir can plausibly supply the same aminonitrile used by the direct alkaline route. Consecutive hydrolysis does not require selective accumulation of valinamide. The additional uncertainty is the rate and extent of reservoir conversion to aminonitrile, rather than any conservation defect. Alkaline hydrothermal processing remains conditional on adequate alkalinity and favorable conversion relative to decomposition.
suggestions: Establish net aminonitrile production from the cyanohydrin-containing mixture rather than inferring it from cyanohydrin disappearance.
Test the transferred reaction mixture under the proposed alkaline hydrothermal conditions, including dilution and mineral interactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acid-to-base sequence is chemically coherent, and valinamide deprotonation is straightforward. Establishing this particular history requires recoverable protonated valinamide after surface hydration and enough base to neutralize the transported acidic solution before alkaline cleavage. The issue is amide survival and acid/base accounting, not the number or order of environments. Continued acidic hydrolysis could instead deliver valine through P1.
suggestions: Measure the amide-containing transfer window and distinguish flux through this history from direct acidic hydrolysis.
Include bulk solution acidity and mineral buffering in the neutralization budget, not only the proton attached to valinamide.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: All transformations have plausible net chemistry, but this history combines uncertain cyanohydrin-reservoir conversion with an unverified amide transfer window. The acid/base reactions are not problematic intrinsically; their successful implementation requires sufficient neutralization capacity and retained substrate. Formation of valine by another overlapping branch would not establish flux through this specific sequence.
suggestions: Track carbon and nitrogen recovery from cyanohydrin through aminonitrile and valinamide.
Test the pH switch using the complete acidic reaction mixture and measure amide recovery and subsequent valinate yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Alkaline hydration followed by protonation and acidic amide cleavage is chemically valid. Its distinctive requirement is that appreciable valinamide survives the initial heated alkaline stage and subsequent transfer. Protonation itself is rapid and credible, but does not establish this kinetic window. Overhydrolysis would divert material toward P3 rather than necessarily prevent network-level valine production.
suggestions: Determine whether valinamide accumulates sufficiently during alkaline hydration to support a measurable transfer flux.
Quantify cooling, transport and acidification recovery, including the acid needed to neutralize the alkaline carrier solution.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route correctly connects the cyanohydrin reservoir to valine through aminonitrile and valinamide. Its uncertainties are net reservoir conversion and survival of the amide during alkaline processing and transfer. The final acidic hydrolysis is standard chemistry under sufficiently forcing conditions, but no substrate-specific conditions or recoveries establish the complete history.
suggestions: Measure reservoir-to-aminonitrile conversion before assigning material to this pathway.
Resolve aminonitrile hydration from subsequent amide cleavage kinetically and test the recovered amide in the acidic compartment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bucherer-Bergs chemistry makes the hydantoin branch plausible, but the supplied surface label does not establish suitable carbon dioxide/carbonate speciation, temperature or conversion. Hydantoin ring opening and acidic decarbamoylation require demonstrated rates; hydantoin re-formation can compete during acidic processing of N-carbamoylvaline. rxn_016 is conservation-valid with two proton equivalents, not an unbalanced reaction.
suggestions: Demonstrate hydantoin formation from valine aminonitrile under the proposed aqueous ammonia/carbon dioxide conditions.
Measure ring opening and decarbamoylation separately, including hydantoin re-formation and decomposition; explicitly write the coefficient 2 for H+ in rxn_016.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The graph provides a valid route from the cyanohydrin reservoir through aminonitrile, hydantoin and N-carbamoylvaline to the target. Nevertheless, reservoir conversion and hydantoin processing are both unverified under the stated environments. The principal terminal uncertainty is successful acidic decarbamoylation rather than simple acidification. rxn_016 balances with two H+ equivalents and has no conservation violation.
suggestions: Track cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile-to-hydantoin conversion with intermediate identification rather than treating reservoir consumption as proof of the sequence.
Specify and test the staged hydrolysis conditions, explicitly accounting for two H+ in rxn_016 and measuring competing cyclization and transport losses.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is connected, has sufficient molecule and reaction nodes, and uses its identifiers and protonation states consistently. The deterministic check establishes that all 16 reactions conserve atoms and charge: 15 are balanced as written, and rxn_016 requires two H+ equivalents. There are no conservation violations. Conventional Strecker chemistry provides credible routes to valine, and formation of a racemate is appropriate without a chiral influence. The net-neutral target can represent aqueous zwitterionic valine. Supplied isobutyraldehyde is a legitimate boundary condition; its unclaimed geochemical synthesis is not penalized. Anoxia, UV shielding and separate confined fractures are compatible with the proposed nonphotochemical chemistry, but do not establish reaction rates or transfer efficiencies. The supplied reaction list lacks reaction-specific numerical temperatures, pressures, pH values, concentrations and residence times. Shared uncertainties include free-cyanide availability, acid/base capacity, competing reactions and transport recovery. The pH-switch histories need demonstrated amide flux, while the hydantoin histories require stronger evidence for formation and terminal hydrolysis under the proposed conditions. Failure to establish an optional processing history would not by itself invalidate valine production through another branch. No research findings or experimental citations were supplied, so condition-specific literature alignment cannot be independently verified. The listed problematic reactions identify kinetic, mechanistic-resolution or environmental uncertainties, not conservation failures. Confidence is not increased by the ten overlapping paths or determined by the number or order of environments. Overall, this is a structurally valid and chemically credible conditional network with notable unresolved environmental and kinetic requirements; it does not meet the network approval threshold of 0.90.
